question: In nursing management, what do we mean by conflict "antecedents"?

options.A: The official disciplinary policies used after a fight occurs
options.B: The underlying conditions that create fertile ground for disputes
options.C: The emotional reactions patients have to hospital staff
options.D: The legal documents signed when a nurse is hired

explanation: Think of antecedents as the early sparks or background conditions that set the stage for a disagreement to happen later. Spotting them early helps you keep the ward peaceful! [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why should a nurse manager pay attention to conflict antecedents instead of only reacting when staff start arguing?

options.A: It addresses the root causes before disputes damage team safety and morale
options.B: It stops managers from having to talk to their staff members
options.C: It is required by hospital law to document every single argument
options.D: It ensures that nurses never disagree on clinical procedures

explanation: Fixing the root causes early stops minor issues from blowing up into full-blown arguments, keeping the ward safe and friendly for everyone. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h1)

question: What does "role ambiguity" mean for a nursing team on the ward?

options.A: Staff members refuse to speak to each other during shifts
options.B: There are not enough wheelchairs available for patients
options.C: The hospital building has confusing hallways and signs
options.D: Nurses are unclear about their exact duties and responsibilities

explanation: Role ambiguity happens when job boundaries are fuzzy. When nobody is quite sure who is supposed to handle a specific task, confusion and frustration naturally follow. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h2)

question: A busy ward has only one working patient lift, and both the day and night shifts keep arguing over who gets to use it. What is driving this conflict?
explanation: When important tools or equipment are in short supply, tension builds up fast. That is classic resource scarcity in action! [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which of these is a common interpersonal trigger for conflict among nurses on a unit?

options.B: The physical temperature of the nursing station

explanation: Rushed handovers and unclear messages easily lead to misunderstandings and hurt feelings between colleagues. Clear talk prevents unnecessary drama! [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h3)

question: Two nurses have totally different working styles, which causes minor daily friction between them. How is the best way to view this?

options.A: One of the nurses must be fired immediately for misconduct
options.B: It is a normal interpersonal clash of styles rather than a moral failure
options.C: The hospital building design is entirely to blame for their frustration
options.D: They will eventually agree on everything if left alone long enough

explanation: People naturally work differently—some are fast-paced, others meticulous. Recognizing this as a simple style difference helps teams manage tension without making it personal. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h3)

question: How does constant stress on a very busy hospital ward affect a nurse's day-to-day interactions?

options.A: It strips away emotional resilience and shortens tempers
options.B: It forces staff to work slower and more carefully
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for formal shift handovers
options.D: It increases patience and tolerance for mistakes

explanation: High workloads and non-stop noise drain mental energy. When everyone is exhausted, even small annoyances can make tempers flare. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h4)

question: A tired nurse snaps at a junior colleague for asking a routine question during a chaotic, understaffed shift. What likely caused this reaction?

options.A: A long-standing personal grudge outside of work
options.B: Severe role ambiguity in the hospital structure
options.D: A fundamental difference in personal moral values

explanation: When a shift is chaotic and exhausting, patience wears thin. It is usually the heavy workload talking, not personal malice. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h4)

question: What are individual and psychological causes of conflict mostly rooted in?

options.A: The official hospital building blueprint and layout
options.C: The exact number of beds available in the ward
options.D: Personal values, perceptions, and individual goals

explanation: These triggers come from within each person—how we view situations, what we value most, and what we personally want to achieve. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h5)

question: Why can having different professional goals cause friction between hospital management and bedside nurses?

options.A: Because differing priorities make each group feel the other is doing things wrong
options.B: Because hospital regulations forbid nurses from talking to administrators
options.C: Because managers want patients to stay in the hospital as long as possible
options.D: Because bedside nurses do not care about hospital budgets

explanation: When management focuses on quick patient turnover and bedside nurses focus on deep clinical care, their differing priorities can make them misunderstand each other. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h5)

question: Which of these is an early warning sign that conflict is brewing on a ward?

options.A: Nurses eagerly volunteering to help each other with heavy tasks
options.B: Staff members starting a shared book club
options.C: An increase in overall patient satisfaction scores
options.D: Passive-aggressive notes and increased sarcasm during handovers

explanation: Sarcasm, eye-rolling, and sticky notes left behind are classic signs that team members are starting to rub each other the wrong way. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h6)

question: Why is it smart for a nurse manager to catch early warning signs instead of waiting for a big formal complaint?

options.A: It proves to the hospital director that the shift is running perfectly
options.B: It allows the manager to punish the guilty nurses immediately
options.C: It ensures that hospital management never has to spend money on training
options.D: It gives the manager a chance to step in before the atmosphere turns toxic

explanation: Catching small tensions early lets you talk it out before it explodes into a major drama that disrupts patient care. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is the main goal of taking proactive steps to manage conflict antecedents?

options.A: To force all nurses to have the exact same personality
options.B: To write up formal disciplinary letters for every mistake
options.C: To remove foundational triggers before arguments start
options.D: To reduce the number of patients admitted to the hospital

explanation: Being proactive means fixing the background issues so that arguments have no room to grow in the first place. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h7)

question: A nurse manager notices constant bickering among staff over shift rosters and fairness. What is the best proactive step to take?

options.A: Scold the entire nursing team during the next morning meeting
options.B: Create a transparent and fair scheduling policy with staff input
options.C: Ban all nurses from discussing their rosters at work
options.D: Ignore the complaints until someone quits their job

explanation: Involving the team to build a clear, fair scheduling system removes the guesswork and perceived injustice that causes roster fights. [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h7)
